source.text: Λέγει μοι· Ἆρον ἀπὸ σεαυτοῦ πᾶσαν ἐπιθυμίαν πονηράν, ἔνδυσαι δὲ τὴν ἐπιθυμίαν τὴν ἀγαθὴν καὶ σεμνήν· ἐνδεδυμένος γὰρ τὴν ἐπιθυμίαν ταύτην μισήσεις τὴν πονηρὰν ἐπιθυμίαν καὶ χαλιναγωγήσεις αὐτὴν καθὼς βούλει. 2. ἀγρία γάρ ἐστιν ἡ ἐπιθυμία ἡ πονηρὰ καὶ δυσκόλως ἡμεροῦται· φοβερὰ γάρ ἐστι καὶ λίαν τῇ ἀγριότητι αὐτῆς δαπανᾷ τοὺς ἀνθρώπους· μάλιστα δὲ ἐὰν ἐμπέσῃ εἰς αὐτὴν δοῦλος Θεοῦ καὶ μὴ ᾖ συνετός, δαπανᾶται ὑπ’ αὐτῆς δεινῶς. δαπανᾷ δὲ τοὺς τοιούτους τοὺς μὴ ἔχοντας ἔνδυμα τῆς ἐπιθυμίας τῆς ἀγαθῆς, ἀλλὰ ἐμπεφυρμένους τῷ αἰῶνι τούτῳ. τούτους οὖν παραδίδωσιν εἰς θάνατον. 3. Ποῖα, φημί, κύριε, ἔργα ἐστὶ τῆς ἐπιθυμίας τῆς πονηρᾶς τὰ παραδιδόντα τοὺς ἀνθρώπους εἰς θάνατον; γνώρισόν μοι, ἵνα ἀφέξομαι ἀπ’ αὐτῶν. Ἄκουσον, [φησίν,] ἐν ποίοις ἔργοις θανατοῖ ἡ ἐπιθυμία ἡ πονηρὰ τοὺς δούλους τοῦ Θεοῦ.

translation.text:
He says to me: “Remove from yourself every evil desire[h], but clothe yourself with the desire that is good and dignified[a]; for when you are clothed with this desire, you will hate the evil desire and you will bridle[b] it as you wish.

2. “For evil desire is wild and is hard to tame; for it is fearsome, and by its savagery it greatly consumes[c] people—especially if a servant of God falls into it and is not sensible, he is grievously consumed by it. It consumes such as these: those who do not have the garment of good desire, but are mixed up with this age[d]. These, therefore, it hands over to death.”

3. “What deeds of evil desire,” I say, “hand people over to death, sir[e]? Make them known to me, so that I may keep away from them.” “Listen,” [he says][f], “by what deeds evil desire puts the servants of God[g] to death.”

source.text: Πάντων προέχουσα ἐπιθυμία γυναικὸς ἀλλοτρίας ἢ ἀνδρός, καὶ πολυτελείας πλούτου καὶ ἐδεσμάτων πολλῶν ματαίων καὶ μεθυσμάτων, καὶ ἑτέρων τρυφῶν πολλῶν καὶ μωρῶν· πᾶσα γὰρ τρυφὴ μωρά ἐστι καὶ κενὴ τοῖς δούλοις τοῦ Θεοῦ. 2. αὗται οὖν αἱ ἐπιθυμίαι πονηραί εἰσι, θανατοῦσαι τοὺς δούλους τοῦ Θεοῦ. αὕτη γὰρ ἡ ἐπιθυμία ἡ πονηρὰ τοῦ διαβόλου θυγάτηρ ἐστίν. ἀπέχεσθαι οὖν δεῖ ἀπὸ τῶν ἐπιθυμιῶν τῶν πονηρῶν, ἵνα ἀποσχόμενοι ζήσητε τῷ Θεῷ. 3. ὅσοι δὲ ἂν κατακυριευθῶσιν ὑπ᾽ αὐτῶν καὶ μὴ ἀντισταθῶσιν αὐταῖς, ἀποθανοῦνται εἰς τέλος· θανατώδεις γάρ εἰσιν αἱ ἐπιθυμίαι αὗται. 4. σὺ δὲ ἔνδυσαι τὴν ἐπιθυμίαν τῆς δικαιοσύνης, καὶ καθοπλισάμενος τὸν φόβον τοῦ Κυρίου ἀντίστηθι αὐταῖς. ὁ γὰρ φόβος τοῦ Θεοῦ κατοικεῖ ἐν τῇ ἐπιθυμίᾳ τῇ ἀγαθῇ. ἡ ἐπιθυμία ἡ πονηρά, ἐὰν ἴδῃ σε καθωπλισμένον τῷ φόβῳ τοῦ Θεοῦ καὶ ἀνθεστηκότα αὐτῇ, φεύξεται ἀπὸ σοῦ μακράν, καὶ οὐκ ἔτι σοι ὀφθήσεται φοβουμένη τὰ ὅπλα σου. 5. σὺ οὖν στεφανωθεὶς κατ᾽ αὐτῆς ἐλθὲ πρὸς τὴν ἐπιθυμίαν τῆς δικαιοσύνης, καὶ παραδοὺς αὐτῇ τὸ νῖκος ὃ ἔλαβες, δούλευσον αὐτῇ καθὼς αὐτὴ βούλεται. ἐὰν δουλεύσῃς τῇ ἐπιθυμίᾳ τῇ ἀγαθῇ καὶ ὑποταγῇς αὐτῇ, δυνήσῃ τῆς ἐπιθυμίας τῆς πονηρᾶς κατακυριεῦσαι καὶ ὑποτάξαι αὐτὴν καθὼς βούλει.

translation.text:
‘Foremost of all is desire for another’s wife or husband[a], and for the luxury of wealth, and for many vain dishes and intoxicating drinks[b], and for many other foolish indulgences[c]; for every indulgence is foolish and empty for the servants of God[d].

2. These, then, are evil desires, putting the servants of God to death. For this evil desire is the devil’s daughter. Therefore one must abstain from evil desires, so that, by abstaining, you may live to God[e].

3. But all who are overmastered by them and do not stand against them will die utterly[f]; for these desires are death‑dealing.

4. But you—put on the desire for righteousness[g], and, having armed yourself with the fear of the Lord, stand against them. For the fear of God dwells in the good desire. If the evil desire sees you armed with the fear of God and standing against it, it will flee far away from you, and it will no longer appear to you, being afraid of your weapons.

5. So then, having been crowned in your contest against it[h], come to the desire for righteousness, and, handing over to it the victory you received, serve it as it wills[i]. If you serve the good desire and submit to it, you will be able to master[j] the evil desire and to subject it as you wish.’

footnotes.text: Greek: “a woman belonging to another or a man.” The rendering makes the symmetry explicit in English.
“Dishes” renders ἐδέσματα (prepared courses), and “intoxicating drinks” renders μεθύσματα. Alternatives: “foods and potations.” “Vain” (ματαῖα) carries the sense of empty, futile.
τρυφή signifies self‑indulgent luxury or soft living. “Indulgences” keeps the moral nuance.
Or “servants of God.” The translation chooses “slaves” to keep the sharp allegiance contrast in this context.
Or “live for God.” The dative is kept as “to God” to preserve the ancient idiom.
εἰς τέλος intensifies the verb: “utterly, to the full.” Alternatives: “die in the end,” “die completely.”
Lit. “desire of righteousness.” Rendered as “for righteousness” to express orientation; Hermas also calls it “the good desire,” personifying it.
στεφανωθείς evokes the victor’s wreath after a contest; κατ’ αὐτῆς marks the adversative direction (“against it”).
“Serve” translates δουλεύω; alternatively, “be a slave to it.” The nuance of devoted service is intended.
“Master” renders κατακυριεῦσαι; alternatives: “gain dominion over,” “overpower.”

lexical_decisions.rationale: The term covers both positive and negative longing in this passage; using “desire” preserves the symmetry between evil desire and the desire aligned with righteousness.

alternatives: a woman belonging to another or a man
another man’s wife or a man
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀλλότριος means “belonging to another.” Rendering symmetrically reflects the moral scope to both sexes, fitting Hermas’s paraenetic style.
πολυτέλεια denotes luxurious living; “luxury” is concise and retains the moral critique.
“Wealth” is the plain modern equivalent and pairs naturally with luxury.
The word often refers to prepared dishes/delicacies; “dishes” keeps the concrete image of many courses.
Hermas frequently uses “vain” in moral critique; it preserves the moral coloring without over-explaining.
μεθύσμα refers to intoxicant drinks; “intoxicating drinks” communicates plainly without archaic tone.
τρυφή connotes soft, luxurious self‑indulgence; “indulgence” captures the moral nuance and fits repeated phrasing.
“Foolish” is the standard moral term and matches Hermas’s register.
Following project policy, “slave” is used where ownership/service is theologically salient; Hermas emphasizes belonging to God over against sinful masters.
“Evil desires” is transparent and preserves moral weight.
The vivid compound emphasizes that such desires inflict death; “death‑dealing” keeps the sharpness.
In early Christian usage διάβολος functions as a proper designation; “the devil” communicates this idiomatically.
“Abstain” is the standard moral term for avoidance of vices and fits Hermas’s exhortational style.
The dative expresses orientation/relationship; “to God” preserves the ancient idiom while remaining intelligible.
Passive sense here: to be mastered by. “Overmastered” captures being brought under power without awkwardness.
Hermas repeats the imagery of standing/opposing; “stand against” keeps the combat metaphor alongside “armed.”
εἰς τέλος intensifies finality; “utterly” communicates completeness without adding interpretation.
Retains the clothing metaphor common in moral exhortation.
Project default retains “righteousness” in non‑forensic exhortation contexts.
The middle participle stresses self‑arming; “arm yourself” aligns with the martial imagery of weapons and fleeing enemies.
“Fear” preserves the moral seriousness and covenantal idiom; softening to “reverence” would blunt the exhortation.
“Dwell” retains the dwelling metaphor and weight of presence.
Explicitly renders both motion and distance implied by μακράν.
“Weapons” matches the active combat scene (arming, fleeing), whereas “armor” would shift the image.

lexical_decisions.chosen: having been crowned in your contest against it
alternatives: having received the victor’s wreath against it
lexical_decisions.rationale: The participle evokes athletic victory and wreath; the added “in your contest” clarifies κατ’ αὐτῆς as adversative without adding new concepts.
Neuter form of ‘victory’ attested in Koine; retaining “victory” keeps the athletic/contest imagery.
“Handing over” is concrete and fits the image of transferring the wreath/win to the good desire’s service.
While the verb can carry slavery nuance, here it balances the previous “slaves of God” without overloading the phrase; footnoted alternative noted in text.
Keeps the contrast: submit to the good desire; subject the evil desire.

alternatives: to gain dominion over … to subdue
lexical_decisions.rationale: “Master/subject” render the different but related verbs without redundancy.
Simple idiomatic English for volition; avoids casual tone of “please.”

theological_decisions.chosen_reading: “slaves of God” in the main text
theological_decisions.rationale: Hermas stresses belonging and mastery (desires enslave; God owns). Using “slaves” preserves the sharpness of allegiance language per project policy.
theological_decisions.doctrine_reference: DOCTRINE.md — Contested terms: doulos → slave where bonded nature is salient.

theological_decisions.chosen_reading: Translate φόβος literally as “fear”
theological_decisions.rationale: The mandate uses martial imagery and threat of death; softening to “reverence” would undercut the exhortational force and the stated indwelling of fear within good desire.

theological_decisions.chosen_reading: Keep the dative as “to God”
theological_decisions.rationale: Maintains the ancient idiom of orientation without adopting ecclesiastical archaism; “to God” avoids interpretive narrowing.

theological_decisions.chosen_reading: Render as “desire for righteousness”
theological_decisions.rationale: The genitive is best taken as objective (desire directed toward righteousness). The personification is maintained elsewhere as “the good desire.”

theological_decisions.chosen_reading: Translate εἰς τέλος as an intensifier of completeness: “utterly.”
theological_decisions.rationale: Preserves the warning’s severity without specifying a doctrinal schema of final death; leaves interpretive space for Hermas’s own soteriology.

theological_decisions.issue: Personifying evil desire as “the devil’s daughter”
theological_decisions.chosen_reading: Retain the familial metaphor literally
theological_decisions.rationale: Hermas’s personification is integral to his moral psychology; “daughter” preserves gendered metaphor and vividness.

theological_decisions.chosen_reading: Keep explicit martial/athletic metaphors
theological_decisions.rationale: The section weaves arming, resisting, fleeing, and wreathing into a coherent exhortation; preserving the metaphors keeps the rhetorical backbone.

review_passes.summary: The draft is highly accurate and captures the moral force of Hermas well. A couple of minor adjustments are suggested: smoothing out the translation of 'many other foolish indulgences' and correcting the conditional 'if' (ἐάν) in verse 4.
issues_found: In verse 1, 'many other indulgences, foolish ones besides' is slightly clunky for ἑτέρων τρυφῶν πολλῶν καὶ μωρῶν. 'Many other foolish indulgences' is more natural and accurate.
In verse 4, 'When the evil desire sees you' translates ἐὰν ἴδῃ σε, which is a conditional ('If the evil desire sees you').

But I do not know whether these commandments can be kept by a human being, for they are very hard.

In reply he says to me: “If you set it before yourself that they can be kept, you will keep them easily, and they will not be hard. But if it has already risen up in your heart that they cannot be kept by a human being, you will not keep them.

Now I say to you: if you do not keep these, but only remember them in passing, you will walk in the commandments of the devil—difficult and bitter and savage and licentious. And do not be afraid of the devil, for he has no power against you; for I will be with you—I, the angel of repentance[a]—who has mastery over him. The devil has only fear, and his fear has no strength. Do not therefore be afraid of him, and he will flee from you.”

Ὁ μὲν ἄνθρωπος, φημί, κύριε, πρόθυμός ἐστι τὰς ἐντολὰς τοῦ Θεοῦ φυλάσσειν, καὶ οὐδείς ἐστιν ὁ μὴ αἰτούμενος παρὰ τοῦ Κυρίου, ἵνα ἐνδυναμωθῇ ἐν ταῖς ἐντολαῖς αὐτοῦ καὶ ὑποταγῇ αὐταῖς· ἀλλ' ὁ διάβολος σκληρός ἐστι καὶ καταδυναστεύει αὐτῶν. 2. Οὐ δύναται, φησί, καταδυναστεύειν τῶν δούλων τοῦ Θεοῦ τῶν ἐξ ὅλης καρδίας ἐλπιζόντων ἐπ' αὐτόν. δύναται ὁ διάβολος ἀντιπαλαῖσαι, καταπαλαῖσαι δὲ οὐ δύναται. ἐὰν οὖν ἀντισταθῆτε αὐτῷ, νικηθεὶς φεύξεται ἀφ' ὑμῶν κατῃσχυμμένος. ὅσοι δέ, φησίν, ἀπόκενοί εἰσι, φοβοῦνται τὸν διάβολον ὡς δύναμιν ἔχοντα. 3. ὅταν ὁ ἄνθρωπος κεράμια ἱκανώτατα γεμίσῃ οἴνου καλοῦ, καὶ ἐν τοῖς κεραμίοις ἐκείνοις ὀλίγα ἀπόκενα ᾖ, ἔρχεται ἐπὶ τὰ κεράμια καὶ οὐ κατανοεῖ τὰ πλήρη· οἶδε γὰρ ὅτι πλήρη εἰσί· κατανοεῖ δὲ τὰ ἀπόκενα, φοβούμενος μήποτε ὤξισαν· ταχὺ γὰρ τὰ ἀπόκενα κεράμια ὀξίζουσι, καὶ ἀπόλλυται ἡ ἡδονὴ τοῦ οἴνου. 4. οὕτω καὶ ὁ διάβολος ἔρχεται ἐπὶ πάντας τοὺς δούλους τοῦ Θεοῦ ἐκπειράζων αὐτούς. ὅσοι οὖν πλήρεις εἰσὶν ἐν τῇ πίστει, ἀνθεστήκασιν αὐτῷ ἰσχυρῶς, κἀκεῖνος ἀποχωρεῖ ἀπ' αὐτῶν μὴ ἔχων τόπον ποῦ εἰσέλθῃ. ἔρχεται οὖν τότε πρὸς τοὺς ἀποκένους, καὶ ἔχων τόπον εἰσπορεύεται εἰς αὐτούς, καὶ ὃ δὲ βούλεται ἐν αὐτοῖς ἐργάζεται, καὶ γίνονται αὐτῷ ὑπόδουλοι.

translation.text:
I say to him[a], "Lord, listen to a few words from me." He says, "Speak what you wish."

"A person," I say, "Lord, is eager to keep the commandments of God, and there is no one who does not ask from the Lord to be strengthened in his commandments and to be made subject to them; but the devil is harsh and tyrannizes them."

"He is not able," he says, "to tyrannize the servants of God—those who put their hope in him with their whole heart. The devil can grapple, but he cannot overthrow. If, therefore, you resist him[b], defeated he will flee from you, disgraced. But those who are empty," he says, "are afraid of the devil as though he had power.

"When a man fills very many clay jars with good wine, and among those jars a few are empty, he comes to the jars and does not examine the full ones—for he knows they are full—but he inspects the empty ones, fearing lest they have turned sour; for empty jars quickly turn sour, and the enjoyment of the wine is lost.

"So also the devil comes upon all the servants of God, putting them to the test. Therefore, as many as are full in faith have strongly resisted him, and he withdraws from them, having no place where he may enter. He comes then to the empty ones; and having a place, he enters into them, and he does in them what he wishes[h][g][f][e][d][c], and they become enslaved to him."

footnotes.text: Empty translates Greek apokenos, "empty, drained, hollow"; here it figuratively contrasts with being "full in faith."
Clay jars renders keramia, common earthenware vessels for wine in antiquity. The note about empty jars souring reflects ancient experience with residues tainting wine.
Putting them to the test translates ekpeirazō; with the devil as subject, "tempting them" is also possible.
Literally, "having no place to enter"; idiomatically, no opening or opportunity.
Grapple/overthrow renders antipalaio/katapalaio, evoking wrestling: he can wrestle but cannot throw down or pin.
Enjoyment renders hēdonē; "pleasure" is a possible alternative.
Or 'I said to him'.
Or '"A person, Lord, is eager'.

Imperative prohibition best rendered with clear, direct English. "Do not be afraid" is natural while preserving the exhortational tone. "Do not fear" is possible but slightly more archaic in register.

Hermas employs διάβολος as the personal adversary figure. "Devil" communicates this conventional referent in early Christian discourse; "accuser/slanderer" would over-literalize and potentially obscure the personal entity intended.
Aorist passive indicative in narrative speech. Simple past "I was sent" fits the context of commission; English present perfect is possible but less direct.
Standard idiom with μετά + genitive meaning "with"; "to be with you" is the most straightforward rendering.
Hebraic/Septuagintal idiom carried into Christian Greek. "With all [their] heart" preserves the biblical register; "wholeheartedly" is acceptable but less transparent to the underlying imagery.
Hermas frequently uses the parenthetic reporting formula φησί in direct discourse. Retaining "he says" in dashes signals the stylistic feature without interrupting readability.

translation.text:
…to establish them in the faith.

Therefore[f], believe God—you who, on account of your sins, have despaired of your life, and are adding sin to sin, and are burdening your life—that if you turn back to the Lord with your whole heart and work righteousness for the remaining days of your life, and serve him rightly according to his will, he will make healing for your former transgressions[b], and you will have power to gain mastery over the works of the devil. And do not at all fear the devil’s threat; for he is strengthless, like the sinews of a dead man[c].

Listen to me, then, and fear the One who is able to do all things, to save and to destroy[d]; and keep these commandments, and you will live to God.

I say to him, “Lord, now I have been strengthened in all the righteous requirements of the Lord, because you are with me; and I know that you will cut off all the devil’s power, and we shall gain mastery over him and prevail against all his works. And I hope, Lord, that now I can keep these commandments that you have commanded, with the Lord strengthening me.”

“You will keep them,” he says, “if the turning is toward your own city[a].

Foolish, double‑minded, and wretched man, do you not understand that all these things are alien, and are under the authority of another? For the lord of this city will say, ‘I do not want you to dwell in my city; rather, go out from this city, because you do not make use of my laws.’ So then, you—having fields and dwellings and many other possessions—when you are cast out by him, what will you do with your field and your house, and the rest of the things you have prepared for yourself? For the lord of this land says to you, rightly, ‘Either make use of my laws, or withdraw from my land.’ So then, what are you about to do, having…[e]

footnotes.text: The Greek reads irregularly, “if the turning (ἡ κάμψαι) is to your own city.” Many editors suspect a scribal lapse (e.g., τό for ἡ, or an omitted μή). The parable that follows supports the sense of orienting toward one’s true city.
Greek ἴασιν can mean healing or cure. Some translations smooth to “forgiveness/remission,” but Hermas’s moral-therapeutic imagery is likely intentional.
In antiquity sinews were a metaphor for strength. Saying the devil is like the sinews of a dead man underscores utter powerlessness.
This phrasing echoes early Christian speech about God as the one able to save and to destroy (cf. echoes in James 4:12; Matt 10:28), though Hermas is not directly quoting.
The Greek text in this source slice breaks off mid-sentence here (“So then, what are you about to do, having…”); the unit continues in the next segment.
Or 'believe in God—you who, on account of your sins, have despaired of your life, and are adding sin to sin, and are burdening your life—for if you turn back'.

theological_decisions.chosen_reading: Render as “turn back to the Lord with your whole heart.”
theological_decisions.rationale: Hermas emphasizes moral reorientation and ongoing obedience, not only cognitive change or a technical conversion term. ‘Turn back’ reflects volition and relational return.

theological_decisions.chosen_reading: “He will make healing for your former transgressions.”
alternative_readings: He will forgive your former sins
He will grant remission of your past sins
theological_decisions.rationale: Hermas’s moral-struggle discourse frequently uses therapeutic metaphors for sin; preserving ‘healing’ maintains that texture without denying the judicial aspect implied by ‘transgressions.’

theological_decisions.chosen_reading: Translate διάβολος as “devil,” preserve the vivid image of impotence “like the sinews of a dead man.”
theological_decisions.rationale: In Hermas, διάβολος functions as the personal adversary. The image underscores the contrast between God’s power and the devil’s threats, fitting the paraenetic aim.

theological_decisions.issue: Dative of reference in “you will live to God”
theological_decisions.chosen_reading: Retain the literal idiom “live to God.”
theological_decisions.rationale: Hermas’s register often mirrors early Christian idiom; rendering the dative preserves that feel and leaves interpretive space for readers.

theological_decisions.chosen_reading: Render both occurrences as “Lord,” leaving the referential tension in place (“Lord” addressed, and “with the Lord strengthening me”).
alternative_readings: Differentiate as ‘master’ for the speaker and ‘Lord’ for God
theological_decisions.rationale: Hermas’s visions often blur angelic agency and divine commission; preserving the lexical sameness reflects that ancient texture rather than resolving it for modern readers.

theological_decisions.issue: Conditional clause on turning to one’s own city
theological_decisions.chosen_reading: “You will keep them … if the turning is toward your own city.”
alternative_readings: if you do not turn aside to your own city
if you turn aside to your own city
theological_decisions.rationale: The transmitted Greek is irregular; the ensuing parable clarifies the sense: one must orient toward one’s true city (God’s realm) rather than invest in the foreign city (this world). The chosen rendering keeps the metaphor’s direction without over-fixing the Greek.

Ὁ μὲν ἄνθρωπος, φημί, κύριε, πρόθυμός ἐστι τὰς ἐντολὰς τοῦ Θεοῦ φυλάσσειν, καὶ οὐδείς ἐστιν ὁ μὴ αἰτούμενος παρὰ τοῦ Κυρίου, ἵνα ἐνδυναμωθῇ ἐν ταῖς ἐντολαῖς αὐτοῦ καὶ ὑποταγῇ αὐταῖς· ἀλλ' ὁ διάβολος σκληρός ἐστι καὶ καταδυναστεύει αὐτῶν. 2. Οὐ δύναται, φησί, καταδυναστεύειν τῶν δούλων τοῦ Θεοῦ τῶν ἐξ ὅλης καρδίας ἐλπιζόντων ἐπ' αὐτόν. δύναται ὁ διάβολος ἀντιπαλαῖσαι, καταπαλαῖσαι δὲ οὐ δύναται. ἐὰν οὖν ἀντισταθῆτε αὐτῷ, νικηθεὶς φεύξεται ἀφ' ὑμῶν κατῃσχυμμένος. ὅσοι δέ, φησίν, ἀπόκενοί εἰσι, φοβοῦνται τὸν διάβολον ὡς δύναμιν ἔχοντα. 3. ὅταν ὁ ἄνθρωπος κεράμια ἱκανώτατα γεμίσῃ οἴνου καλοῦ, καὶ ἐν τοῖς κεραμίοις ἐκείνοις ὀλίγα ἀπόκενα ᾖ, ἔρχεται ἐπὶ τὰ κεράμια καὶ οὐ κατανοεῖ τὰ πλήρη· οἶδε γὰρ ὅτι πλήρη εἰσί· κατανοεῖ δὲ τὰ ἀπόκενα, φοβούμενος μήποτε ὤξισαν· ταχὺ γὰρ τὰ ἀπόκενα κεράμια ὀξίζουσι, καὶ ἀπόλλυται ἡ ἡδονὴ τοῦ οἴνου. 4. οὕτω καὶ ὁ διάβολος ἔρχεται ἐπὶ πάντας τοὺς δούλους τοῦ Θεοῦ ἐκπειράζων αὐτούς. ὅσοι οὖν πλήρεις εἰσὶν ἐν τῇ πίστει, ἀνθεστήκασιν αὐτῷ ἰσχυρῶς, κἀκεῖνος ἀποχωρεῖ ἀπ' αὐτῶν μὴ ἔχων τόπον ποῦ εἰσέλθῃ. ἔρχεται οὖν τότε πρὸς τοὺς ἀποκένους, καὶ ἔχων τόπον εἰσπορεύεται εἰς αὐτούς, καὶ ὃ δὲ βούλεται ἐν αὐτοῖς ἐργάζεται, καὶ γίνονται αὐτῷ ὑπόδουλοι.

Οὐ δύναται, φησί, καταδυναστεύειν τῶν δούλων τοῦ Θεοῦ τῶν ἐξ ὅλης καρδίας ἐλπιζόντων ἐπ' αὐτόν. δύναται ὁ διάβολος ἀντιπαλαῖσαι, καταπαλαῖσαι δὲ οὐ δύναται. ἐὰν οὖν ἀντισταθῆτε αὐτῷ, νικηθεὶς φεύξεται ἀφ' ὑμῶν κατῃσχυμμένος. ὅσοι δέ, φησίν, ἀπόκενοί εἰσι, φοβοῦνται τὸν διάβολον ὡς δύναμιν ἔχοντα. 3. ὅταν ὁ ἄνθρωπος κεράμια ἱκανώτατα γεμίσῃ οἴνου καλοῦ, καὶ ἐν τοῖς κεραμίοις ἐκείνοις ὀλίγα ἀπόκενα ᾖ, ἔρχεται ἐπὶ τὰ κεράμια καὶ οὐ κατανοεῖ τὰ πλήρη· οἶδε γὰρ ὅτι πλήρη εἰσί· κατανοεῖ δὲ τὰ ἀπόκενα, φοβούμενος μήποτε ὤξισαν· ταχὺ γὰρ τὰ ἀπόκενα κεράμια ὀξίζουσι, καὶ ἀπόλλυται ἡ ἡδονὴ τοῦ οἴνου. 4. οὕτω καὶ ὁ διάβολος ἔρχεται ἐπὶ πάντας τοὺς δούλους τοῦ Θεοῦ ἐκπειράζων αὐτούς. ὅσοι οὖν πλήρεις εἰσὶν ἐν τῇ πίστει, ἀνθεστήκασιν αὐτῷ ἰσχυρῶς, κἀκεῖνος ἀποχωρεῖ ἀπ' αὐτῶν μὴ ἔχων τόπον ποῦ εἰσέλθῃ. ἔρχεται οὖν τότε πρὸς τοὺς ἀποκένους, καὶ ἔχων τόπον εἰσπορεύεται εἰς αὐτούς, καὶ ὃ δὲ βούλεται ἐν αὐτοῖς ἐργάζεται, καὶ γίνονται αὐτῷ ὑπόδουλοι.

translation.text: Therefore, believe God—you who, on account of your sins, have despaired of your life, and are adding sins and weighing down your life—that if you turn back to the Lord with your whole heart and work righteousness for the remaining days of your life, and serve him rightly according to his will, he will bring healing to your former sins, and you will have power to gain mastery over the works of the devil. And do not at all fear the devil’s threat; for he is powerless, like the sinews of a dead man.
